notes.meaning: Jewish time was measured from sunrise, so the third hour was about nine o'clock in the morning. At this hour, Roman soldiers nailed Jesus to the wooden cross. Even while human leaders rushed to kill Him, God's saving plan was moving ahead on schedule.

The soldiers fastened a written notice above Jesus' head showing the crime He was accused of committing. Pilate wrote it to insult Jesus and mock the Jewish leaders, yet it stated the absolute truth. Jesus truly is the King who rules by giving His life for His people.

Two violent rebels were executed on crosses beside Jesus, placing Him right in the middle. The authorities did this to treat Him as if He were the worst criminal in the group. He willingly hung in the place of sinners to bear their shame.

This statement points back to the prophet Isaiah, who said the Servant of God would be counted among lawbreakers. Although Jesus never committed any sin, He took the place of guilty people so they could be forgiven. God's ancient word was fulfilled in the way Jesus died.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Most scholars note that this verse is absent from the oldest Greek manuscripts and was likely copied into Mark from Luke 22:37 by later scribes.

notes.meaning: People walking past the cross shook their heads in contempt and threw Jesus' earlier words back at Him. They mocked His claim about rebuilding the temple in three days, assuming the cross proved He had no power. They did not realize that by refusing to save Himself, He was preparing to rise and build God's true spiritual temple.

The chief priests and teachers of the law ridiculed Jesus, saying they would only believe in Him if He performed a miracle and climbed down. Without meaning to, they admitted that He had truly healed and helped others during His ministry. If Jesus had saved Himself from physical death, He could not have saved the world from sin. Even the dying bandits crucified next to Him joined in the insults at first.

At noon, when the sun should have been at its highest, a strange darkness covered the land for three full hours until three in the afternoon. This was not an ordinary eclipse, but a miraculous sign from God showing both His sorrow and His judgment against human sin. Creation itself grew dark while the Son of God carried the heavy curse of our wrongdoing.

Jesus cried out loudly in Aramaic, quoting the opening line of Psalm 22. In this painful moment, He bore the full burden of our sin and experienced real, terrifying separation from the comforting presence of His Father. Even through this deep agony, He showed complete trust by calling out, 'My God, My God.'

Some people standing nearby misheard Jesus' cry and thought He was calling for the ancient prophet Elijah to come rescue Him. A man ran and soaked a sponge with cheap, sour wine, lifting it up on a stalk to moisten Jesus' lips and see what would happen. Even in His final breaths, the crowd treated His suffering like entertainment.

Crucifixion victims normally ran out of air and died in a whisper, but Jesus gave a loud, powerful shout before taking His last breath. This showed that His life was not simply stolen from Him; He willingly gave up His spirit once His work was finished. His suffering came to an end, and the price for sin was paid.

The heavy curtain inside the temple, which kept ordinary people out of God's most holy presence, suddenly tore in two from top to bottom. Because it tore from the very top, it showed that God Himself had torn it open. Through the death of Jesus, the barrier between God and sinners was removed forever.

A Roman centurion was an officer commanding one hundred soldiers, and this man stood directly in front of the cross. He had watched many criminals die, but the darkness, the loud shout, and Jesus' manner convinced him this was no ordinary man. This pagan soldier was the first person after Jesus' death to openly confess that He was truly the Son of God.

A group of faithful women stood watching the cross from a safe distance when most of the male disciples had run away in fear. These women had traveled with Jesus, helped provide for His daily needs in Galilee, and stayed loyal all the way to Jerusalem. Their quiet devotion made them honored witnesses to the crucifixion.

Late afternoon arrived on Friday, which was the preparation day before the weekly Jewish Sabbath began at sunset. Jewish law forbade leaving a dead body hanging on a tree overnight, especially with the holy Sabbath coming. Someone had to act quickly before sundown to give Jesus a proper burial.

Joseph was an honorable member of the Jewish high court who had been quietly waiting for God's promised kingdom to arrive. Though he had followed Jesus secretly before, he gathered his courage and went straight to the Roman governor to ask for the body. He risked his social standing and his safety to show honor to the Lord.

Men on crosses usually lingered for several days, so Pilate was surprised to hear that Jesus was dead after only six hours. He called the centurion who oversaw the execution to confirm the report before doing anything. When the officer assured him that Jesus was truly dead, Pilate released the body to Joseph, creating an official record of Jesus' death.

Joseph bought a clean linen sheet, carefully took the body of Jesus down, and wrapped Him for burial. He placed Jesus inside a new tomb carved out of solid rock and rolled a large stone across the entrance to seal it. Even in death, God saw to it that His Son was treated with honor and laid in a rich man's tomb.

Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joseph sat nearby and watched exactly where the body was laid. They took careful note of the spot so they could return with spices to finish preparing the body once the Sabbath ended. Their watchful eyes provided trustworthy witnesses that Jesus was really placed in that specific tomb.
